gap: The distance metric d(.,.) for nearest-neighbor token scoring is only given as an example ('e.g., Euclidean distance'); cosine or other metrics would change the scores and the AUROC values.
options: Euclidean (L2) distance
cosine distance
negative inner product / dot product
chosen: Euclidean (L2) distance on unnormalized BERT embeddings
rationale: Euclidean is the only metric the paper names explicitly in Eq. (2) discussion, and it is the default in the arXiv PatchCore-style nearest-neighbor scoring the method adapts.
quote: d(·, ·) denotes the distance metric (e.g., Euclidean distance)

gap: Whether the memory bank stores every normal training token embedding or is subsampled (PatchCore uses greedy coreset subsampling), which changes both runtime and AUROC.
options: Full memory bank of all normal training tokens
Random subsample of tokens
Greedy coreset subsampling as in PatchCore
chosen: Full memory bank of all normal training token embeddings
rationale: The paper states the bank has exactly N entries equal to the total number of normal training tokens and never mentions coreset selection, subsampling or FAISS/approximate search being used in the experiments.

gap: Which BERT representations are used: the paper only says 'BERT-base-uncased embeddings' without specifying the hidden layer or whether layers are summed/averaged.
options: Last hidden layer output
Average of the last four hidden layers
Concatenation of several layers
chosen: Last hidden layer output per subword token
rationale: Standard convention for BERT feature extraction and the simplest reading of 'BERT-base-uncased embeddings'.
quote: we first obtain contextualized representations using pre-trained language models such as BERT

gap: How special tokens and punctuation are handled: whether [CLS]/[SEP] and punctuation are stored in the memory bank and scored as tokens, since token-level ground truth only covers words.
options: Exclude [CLS]/[SEP] and punctuation from memory bank and scoring
Include all WordPiece-derived word units, only excluding [CLS]/[SEP]
Score only tokens that carry gold labels
chosen: Exclude [CLS]/[SEP]; keep punctuation-attached word units consistent with the word-level tokenization used for labels
rationale: Token-level annotation is word-level, so scoring must be restricted to word units aligned with the annotation; otherwise the AUROC denominators change.
quote: we need to aggregate subword embeddings to obtain word-level representations for alignment with token-level annotations

gap: How token-level AUROC is aggregated: pooled over all test tokens across documents, or computed per document and averaged, which can shift the reported value substantially under extreme class imbalance.
options: Pool all test tokens of all test documents into one ranking
Average per-document AUROC
Micro-average weighted by document length
chosen: Pool all test tokens of all test documents into one ranking (micro over tokens)
rationale: The paper stresses extreme token-level class imbalance and reports a single per-dataset token-level number without describing per-document averaging.

gap: The SMS_Spam corruption protocol is only described qualitatively: how many messages are corrupted, how much of each message is replaced, the injected sequence length, and the random seed are not specified, so the exact anomaly rate of 8.7% cannot be reconstructed deterministically.
options: Reproduce the released corrupted split from the HuggingFace dataset
Re-run the described injection with a fixed seed targeting 393/4,518 anomalous documents
Re-run with random seed and accept rate drift
chosen: Use the released annotated split if available; otherwise re-run injection with a fixed seed calibrated to 393 anomalous of 4,518 documents (8.7%)
rationale: Only the target counts (393/4,518, 8.7%) are pinned down in the paper, so the sampling must be calibrated to those counts to be comparable.
quote: we randomly select portions of normal messages and inject meaningless character sequences such as ‘jasdhnjsdb’

gap: The Restaurant Review dataset was collected by the authors from Google Maps and no download link is given, so the Review results (0.8271 token / 0.9594 document AUROC) may not be reproducible from public data.
options: Obtain the released Review split from the TokenCore GitHub repository
Substitute a different public review/anomaly corpus
Drop the Review claims from the reproduction
chosen: Obtain the released Review data from the TokenCore repository (https://github.com/charles-cao/TokenCore); if unavailable, mark Review claims as not reproducible
rationale: The paper claims 'All the codes and data are publicly available' at that URL, which is the only plausible public source for this private collection.
quote: This dataset targets semantic anomalies within customer reviews, specifically focusing on negative sentiment expressions embedded in review text.

gap: Which 50% of the normal documents form the training set, and with what seed, is not stated; under small datasets (Grammar has only 300 documents) the split randomness changes AUROC appreciably.
options: Fixed seed (e.g., 0/42) with one split
Multiple random splits averaged
Stratified split by anomaly rate
chosen: Fixed seed with a single random split, repeated over a few seeds to report spread if budget allows
rationale: The paper reports a single number per cell with no std, implying one split; a fixed seed makes the run reproducible.

gap: Whether embeddings are L2-normalized before nearest-neighbor search (which matters for Euclidean vs cosine equivalence) is never stated.
options: No normalization (raw BERT hidden states)
L2-normalize each token embedding before scoring
chosen: No normalization; raw BERT hidden states with Euclidean distance
rationale: The paper describes nearest-neighbor distance in the embedding space with no preprocessing step mentioned.

gap: How the document-level baselines are defined: whether LOF/iForest/ECOD/DeepSVDD/AE/LUNAR are run on document-level mean-pooled embeddings, or on the same token-level scores aggregated by mean as for TokenCore.
options: Run each detector on document-level embeddings
Aggregate token-level detector scores by mean as in Eq. (3)
chosen: Aggregate token-level detector scores by mean (uniform scoring and aggregation for all methods)
rationale: The paper states all methods operate on the same BERT-base-uncased + max pooling representations and TokenCore's document score is a mean of token scores, implying a single shared pipeline.
quote: All the methods operate on BERT-base-uncased embeddings with max pooling aggregation.

gap: Which 270 correct and 30 incorrect sentences were selected for the Grammar benchmark (source Kaggle set is larger) and how they were sampled is unspecified.
options: Use the released Grammar split from the TokenCore repository
Randomly sample 270/30 from the Kaggle grammar-correction pairs with a fixed seed
chosen: Use the released split if available; otherwise sample 270 correct / 30 incorrect with a fixed seed
rationale: Only the final counts (270/30) are stated; sampling must match those counts to reproduce the reported AUROC.
quote: We construct our evaluation set by selecting 270 correct sentences as normal samples and 30 incorrect sentences as anomalous samples
